title: Permutations
description: Given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers, return every ordering of its elements. The permutations themselves may be listed in any order.
hints: Fix the first element, then permute the rest. How do you keep track of which elements are still available?
Carry a `used` boolean array (or a set). At each depth, try every unused element, mark it, recurse, unmark it.
Space-saving variant: swap nums[i] into position `depth`, recurse on depth + 1, then swap back. No extra `used` array.
approach:
**Key insight: a permutation is built position by position, and at each position any element not yet placed is a legal choice.** That is a depth-n search tree with n! leaves.

**Algorithm.** Keep `path` and a parallel `used` array. At each call, if `path` is full record a copy; otherwise for every index `i` with `used[i]` false: mark it, append `nums[i]`, recurse, then undo both. The undo step is what makes it backtracking rather than a copy-everything approach.

**Why it works.** Each leaf corresponds to one injective assignment of elements to positions, i.e. one permutation, and the `used` array guarantees injectivity.

**Common mistakes:** forgetting to reset `used[i]`; appending `path` without copying; using `x in path` for the membership test (O(n) per check and wrong if values could repeat).

**Interview follow-ups:** Duplicates in the input? (sort, and skip `nums[i]` when it equals `nums[i-1]` and `used[i-1]` is false.) Generate the k-th permutation directly? (factorial number system, O(n^2).) Produce the next permutation in place in O(n)? (find the rightmost ascent, swap, reverse the suffix.)

complexity.space: O(n) for recursion and the used array, excluding output
